chapters.title: Baranagore, 1886
chapters.src: Eastern & Western Disciples ch. 12 · Biography ch. 5
lines: After Ramakrishna's passing, his young disciples took a crumbling house at Baranagore, said to be haunted.
Some days there was rice but no salt. For months they lived on rice, salt, and boiled leaves.
And they argued for hours: Kant, Hegel, Mill and Spencer, against the six systems of India.
One day Naren would prove that God was a myth. The next, that God was the only reality.

chapters.title: Persian, Latin, German
lines: How had the Upanishads reached German philosophy at all?
The Mughal prince Dara Shikoh had them translated into Persian.
A Latin version reached Europe, and Schopenhauer read it. His philosophy, Vivekananda said, was moulded by it.
Next to him, he said, the philosophy of Kant also shows traces of the Upanishads.

chapters.title: Two infinites
lines: Two ancient peoples, he said, looked for the infinite in different directions.
The Greeks, surrounded by beauty, studied the outer infinite. The macrocosm.
India, surrounded by the sublime, studied the inner infinite. The microcosm.
Neither needed to borrow from the other. But if they compared notes, both would gain.

chapters.title: The wandering monk
chapters.src: Biography ch. 5 · Eastern & Western Disciples ch. 19
lines: In eighteen ninety, Naren left with a staff and a begging bowl, and the dust of India swallowed him.
Varanasi, Vrindavan, the Himalayas, Rajputana, Gujarat, Mysore, Travancore, and at last, Kanyakumari.
In Madras a disciple marvelled at his range: from the Rig Veda to Kant and Hegel, from Yoga to a modern laboratory.
On the thirty-first of May, eighteen ninety-three, he sailed from Bombay for the West.

chapters.title: Mud puddles
chapters.src: The Vedanta in All Its Phases (CW vol. 3)
lines: Back in Calcutta, he named the German he trusted least: Hegel.
Hegel's idea, he said, is that the Absolute is only chaos, and the individual form is greater. The world is greater than the non-world.
India's answer: every manifestation is a vain attempt of the unmanifested to show itself, like the sun trying to reflect itself in little mud puddles.
After a time it beats a retreat to where it came from. That, he said, is renunciation, the beginning of religion.

chapters.title: Kiel, 1896
lines: In eighteen ninety-six, Professor Paul Deussen invited him to Kiel. Deussen was a disciple of Schopenhauer, and a follower of Kant.
He spoke Sanskrit, and called the Vedanta one of the most majestic structures of the human mind.
Once, absorbed in a book of poems, the Swami did not hear his host. Then he recited the verses back to him.
Deussen foresaw India becoming the spiritual leader of the nations.

chapters.title: Lectures on Maya
lines: In London he gave three lectures on Maya. Some listeners, it is said, were moved to tears.
A white-haired philosopher told him: you have spoken splendidly, but you have told us nothing new.
He answered: Sir, I have told you the Truth. And the Truth is as old as the hills.
If I have told it in words that make you think, and live up to your thinking, do I not do well?

chapters.title: On deck, 1899
chapters.src: Eastern & Western Disciples ch. 35 · Nivedita ch. 15
lines: In June eighteen ninety-nine he sailed again, with Sister Nivedita, on the Golconda.
At Madras, plague kept every Indian passenger aboard. The monsoon tossed them for ten days to Aden.
On deck he set Kant's time, space and causation beside the Vaisheshika categories, and the logic of the Nyaya.
One side gives priority to the outer thing, he said, the other to the inner idea. That problem has no solution.

chapters.title: Messina must thank me
chapters.src: Eastern & Western Disciples ch. 35 · contrast: Chevreul, 1839
lines: Off Sicily, Etna was in eruption, and the moon rose over the Straits of Messina.
Beauty, he told Nivedita, is not outside. It is already in the mind.
Look at these two grey squares. They are the very same grey. The surroundings make one look darker.
Messina must thank me, he laughed. It is I who give her all her beauty.

chapters.title: The Reality behind it
lines: Crossing the Atlantic that August, he paced the deck under a full moon.
If all this Maya is so beautiful, he said, think of the wondrous beauty of the Reality behind it.
And pointing to the sea and sky: why recite poetry, when there is the very essence of poetry?

chapters.title: Arise, awake
chapters.src: Raja-Yoga, Introduction · Calcutta Address and Reply
lines: The boy who studied Kant in Calcutta had carried the question around the world.
Kant showed that time, space and causation are forms of the mind. The Upanishads added: what lies beyond them is your own Self.
From whom all this universe comes out, in whom all that is born lives, and to whom all returns.
Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached.
